title: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
summary: Why neurons are polysemantic, how a wide sparse autoencoder recovers feature directions, how L1, TopK and JumpReLU enforce sparsity, how to handle dead latents, and how to measure and steer with SAE features.
outcomes: Explain superposition and why sparsity lets a layer hold more features than dimensions
Write the SAE encoder, decoder and loss, and explain why decoder norms enter the sparsity penalty
Explain L1 shrinkage and how TopK, Gated and JumpReLU SAEs avoid it
Diagnose dead latents and feature splitting, and choose fixes such as AuxK and resampling
Compute L0 and FVU, interpret downstream loss, and steer a model by clamping a latent

lessons.title: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition

blocks.md:
In the GPT you built, every token carries a vector through the network: the residual stream of width `d_model`, and inside each block an MLP layer with a few thousand neurons. Interpretability asks what those numbers mean. The obvious plan is to read neurons one at a time: find the inputs that make neuron 227 fire and give it a name.

That plan mostly fails in language models. Many neurons are **polysemantic**: they fire for several unrelated things. In Anthropic's one-layer transformer, the neuron most correlated with a clean DNA-sequence feature had DNA as only a tiny sliver of its top activating examples.

blocks.caption: An activation vector x is a bias plus a sum of feature directions d_i, each scaled by how strongly feature i is present. Most f_i are zero on any given token.

blocks.md: Why can a $d$-dimensional space hold more than $d$ useful directions? Only $d$ vectors can be exactly orthogonal, but in high dimensions random directions are **almost** orthogonal. For two random unit vectors in $d$ dimensions the mean squared cosine is exactly $1/d$, so the typical cosine is about $1/\sqrt{d}$. The overlap between two feature directions is called **interference**: when one feature fires, every overlapping feature looks slightly active too.

blocks.title: Typical overlap between random directions shrinks with width

y.label: RMS cosine of two random unit vectors

scenes.caption: The curve is the exact RMS cosine 1/sqrt(d). Dots are a simulation with 2,000 random pairs per width; they sit on the curve.
At d = 2 two random directions overlap heavily (about 0.7). At GPT-2 small's width of 768 the typical overlap is about 0.035, so many nearly independent directions fit.

blocks.md:
Toy Models makes this concrete with a tiny network. Five features $x_1..x_5$ (each zero with high probability, otherwise uniform in $[0,1]$) are squeezed into a 2-dimensional hidden vector and decoded back:

$h = Wx$, then $x' = \text{ReLU}(W^T h + b)$.

$W$ is a 2 by 5 matrix whose columns are the feature directions. When the features are sparse, the paper's trained models place the five directions on a **pentagon**. Below we use a hand-built pentagon (unit vectors 72 degrees apart) so every number can be checked.

blocks.title: Interference matrix W^T W for five features on a pentagon

scenes.caption: Entry (i, j) is the cosine between directions i and j. The diagonal is 1: each feature reads itself back perfectly.
Neighbours on the pentagon overlap by +0.309 (cos 72 degrees). This is positive interference: f1 firing makes f2 and f5 look slightly on.
Non-neighbours overlap by -0.809. Negative interference is harmless here because the output ReLU clips negative values to zero.

blocks.title: Decoding the pentagon with bias b = -0.309 and a ReLU

scenes.caption: Only f1 is on (value 1). Before the ReLU the output is W^T W x: f1 reads 1.0, but f2 and f5 leak +0.309. f3 and f4 read -0.809: bar height shows size, the label shows the sign.
Adding b = -0.309 and applying the ReLU wipes out the leak. f1 comes back as 0.691: a bit shrunk, but no false features.
f1 and its neighbour f2 both on. Pre-activations are 1.309 and 1.309; after the bias both read exactly 1.0. Adjacent pairs decode cleanly.
f1 and f3 both on. Pre-activations are 0.191, 0.618, 0.191: after the bias the true features vanish and f2, which is off, reads 0.309. Interference wins.

blocks.prompt: If each of the five features is independently active with probability p, how often do two or more fire at once (the case that can break the pentagon)? Guess for p = 0.5 and p = 0.05.
blocks.reveal:
From $1-(1-p)^5-5p(1-p)^4$:

- p = 0.5: 81% of inputs have two or more features on, so superposition is costly.
- p = 0.1: 8.2%.
- p = 0.05: 2.3%.
- p = 0.01: 0.1%.

Sparsity makes collisions rare, which is why Toy Models finds that sparse features get stored in superposition while dense ones get a dedicated orthogonal dimension or are dropped.

blocks.md:
Toy Models reports a **phase change**: as sparsity rises, a feature switches from not represented, to represented in superposition, to (if important enough) represented on its own dimension. In the paper's version where the five features differ in importance, dense features get an orthogonal basis for only the two most important ones, much like PCA.

The consequence for interpretability: if a real model works this way, its neurons are the wrong unit of analysis. We need a method that finds the feature directions themselves. That is what a sparse autoencoder does.

Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

Superposition is a hypothesis with strong toy-model evidence, not a proven fact about every layer of every LLM. The pentagon above is hand-built for clean numbers; trained toy models find it too, but their exact weights and biases differ.

blocks.question: A colleague says: 'If a model had 768 dimensions, it could track at most 768 features without errors, so superposition can't help.' What is the best reply?
options: Right: superposition only works when features are dense and frequently co-occur.
Exact orthogonality caps it at 768, but many sparse features can share almost-orthogonal directions because they rarely fire together, and a ReLU filters small interference.
Wrong: 768 dimensions can hold 768 squared exactly orthogonal directions.
Right: that is why language models need one neuron per feature.
blocks.explain: Only d directions can be exactly orthogonal, but random directions in 768 dimensions overlap by only about 0.036. When features are sparse, two overlapping features are rarely on together, and a negative bias plus ReLU removes the small leaks. Dense features make collisions common, which is when superposition stops paying.

blocks.question: In the pentagon model, which input is decoded wrongly with b = -0.309?
options: Only f1 on
f1 and f2 on (neighbours)
f1 and f3 on (non-neighbours)
No feature on
blocks.explain: Non-neighbours have cosine -0.809, so their sum cancels most of each one's own signal (0.191 each) while the shared neighbour f2 gets 0.618. After the bias only f2 survives. Neighbours reinforce each other instead.

lessons.title: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations

blocks.md:
A **sparse autoencoder (SAE)** is a separate, small network trained to rewrite one layer's activations as a sparse sum of learned directions. The language model stays frozen. You run it over a large text corpus, save the activation vector $\mathbf{x}$ at one site (an MLP output, or the residual stream at some layer) for every token, then train the SAE on those vectors.

The SAE has one hidden layer that is much **wider** than $\mathbf{x}$: $M \gg d$ hidden units called **latents**. Each latent owns one decoder column, its dictionary direction. A sparsity penalty makes only a handful of latents fire per token, which is exactly the superposition picture from lesson 1 run in reverse.

blocks.caption: Encoder: subtract a learned centre b_dec, project to M latents, ReLU. Decoder: a linear map back to d dimensions. Column i of W_dec (written d_i) is latent i's direction. This is the Towards Monosemanticity form.

blocks.title: Where the SAE sits and what it computes

scenes.caption: Activations are collected from a frozen model, token by token. Towards Monosemanticity used 8 billion MLP activation vectors from a one-layer transformer.
The encoder projects x into M latents, many more than d. The ReLU zeroes every latent whose pre-activation is negative.
The decoder adds up the directions of the active latents. Few latents fire, so x-hat is a sparse combination of dictionary vectors.
Training pushes two ways: reconstruct x well (MSE) and keep f sparse. The tension between them is the whole design problem of the next lesson.

blocks.caption: The L1-style loss used in Scaling Monosemanticity. lambda sets the trade-off: larger lambda gives fewer active latents and worse reconstruction.

blocks.md:
Why multiply each $f_i$ by its decoder norm $\|\mathbf{d}_i\|$? Without it the SAE can cheat: halve every $f_i$ and double every $\mathbf{d}_i$, and the reconstruction is unchanged while the penalty halves. Towards Monosemanticity blocked this by forcing decoder columns to unit norm; Scaling Monosemanticity instead puts the norm inside the penalty and reports $f_i \|\mathbf{d}_i\|$ as the feature activation.

**Worked example.** Take the pentagon from lesson 1 as a ready-made dictionary: five unit decoder columns in $d = 2$, encoder rows equal to the same directions (tied weights, as in Cunningham et al.), $\mathbf{b}_{dec} = 0$, $\mathbf{b}_{enc} = -0.309$. Feed it the activation produced by feature 1 at strength 0.8: $\mathbf{x} = (0.8, 0)$.

scenes.caption: Input: the 2-d activation (0.8, 0). Five latents, one per pentagon direction.
Encoder pre-activations are dot products with each direction: 0.8 for latent 0, and interference of 0.247 on its two neighbours.
Add b_enc = -0.309 and ReLU: neighbours drop below zero and switch off. Only latent 0 fires (L0 = 1), but at 0.491 instead of 0.8.
Decode: x-hat = 0.491 times direction 0 = (0.491, 0). Squared error is 0.309 squared = 0.095. The right latent fired, but it was shrunk.

blocks.prompt: The bias that silenced the false latents also shrank the true one by exactly 0.309. Is that a coincidence of this example, or a general problem with 'ReLU plus a negative bias' as a way to get sparsity?
blocks.reveal: It is general. A ReLU with bias $b$ subtracts the same amount from every active latent, so the one knob both filters noise and biases the magnitude down. Real L1-trained SAEs show the same effect, called **shrinkage**. Lesson 3 shows how TopK and JumpReLU separate 'which latents fire' from 'how big they are'.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class SAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, M):
        super().__init__()
        self.W_enc = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(M, d) * 0.01)
        self.b_enc = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(M))
        self.W_dec = nn.Parameter(self.W_enc.data.T.clone())  # init dec = enc^T
        self.b_dec = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d))

    def forward(self, x):                      # x: [batch, d]
        f = torch.relu((x - self.b_dec) @ self.W_enc.T + self.b_enc)
        x_hat = f @ self.W_dec.T + self.b_dec  # [batch, d]
        return f, x_hat

def sae_loss(sae, x, lam):
    f, x_hat = sae(x)
    mse = ((x - x_hat) ** 2).sum(-1).mean()
    dec_norms = sae.W_dec.norm(dim=0)          # one norm per latent
    sparsity = (f * dec_norms).sum(-1).mean()
    return mse + lam * sparsity
blocks.caption: A minimal L1 SAE in PyTorch following the equations above. Real training adds activation normalisation, large batches and dead-latent handling.

blocks.md:
Sizes in published work:

- **Towards Monosemanticity** (Anthropic, 2023): a 512-neuron MLP in a one-layer transformer, dictionaries from 512 (1x) to 131,072 (256x) latents.
- **Cunningham et al.** (2023): residual streams of Pythia-70M and Pythia-410M.
- **Scaling Monosemanticity** (Anthropic, 2024): the middle-layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, with about 1M, 4M and 34M latents.
- **Scaling and evaluating SAEs** (OpenAI, 2024): 16 million latents on GPT-4, trained on 40 billion tokens.
- **Gemma Scope** (Google DeepMind, 2024): more than 400 open SAEs covering every layer and sublayer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, with over 30 million latents in total.

An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one.

blocks.question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
blocks.explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

blocks.question: You train an SAE on layer 6 residual-stream activations of your GPT. Which statement is true?
options: The GPT's weights are updated so its neurons become monosemantic
The SAE has fewer hidden units than d_model so it compresses the activations
The GPT is frozen; the SAE learns a wider, sparse re-description of the saved layer 6 vectors
The SAE is trained on next-token cross-entropy only
blocks.explain: The SAE is a separate model trained on stored activations. It is overcomplete (M much larger than d) and trained with a reconstruction plus sparsity objective, not by changing the language model.

lessons.title: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU

blocks.md:
What we really want to penalise is the number of active latents, the **L0 norm** $\|\mathbf{f}\|_0$. L0 is a count, so it has zero gradient almost everywhere and cannot be trained directly with plain backprop. The first SAEs used the **L1 norm** $\sum_i |f_i|$ as a differentiable stand-in.

L1 has a side effect. It charges for **size**, not just for being on, so the optimiser pays to make every active latent a little smaller than the data wants. This is **shrinkage**: systematic underestimation of feature activations (Gated SAE paper; Wright and Sharkey).

blocks.caption: One latent with a unit decoder direction and true strength a. The L1 optimum is always lambda/2 short of the truth.

blocks.title: Shrinkage: the L1 optimum sits lambda/2 below the true activation

scenes.caption: With lambda = 0 both curves coincide and the best f equals a = 0.8. No sparsity pressure, no bias.
lambda = 0.3: the minimum moves to f = 0.65. The reconstruction error 0.15 squared = 0.023 is paid on every token where this latent fires.
lambda = 0.6: f = 0.5, error 0.09. Raising lambda buys sparsity (weak latents switch off entirely) but shrinks every surviving one.

blocks.md: **TopK SAEs** (Gao et al., OpenAI 2024, building on k-sparse autoencoders by Makhzani and Frey) drop the penalty. The encoder keeps only the $k$ largest pre-activations and zeroes the rest; the loss is reconstruction MSE alone. Benefits reported in the paper: no L1 shrinkage, L0 is set directly instead of tuned through $\lambda$, a better sparsity versus reconstruction frontier than ReLU SAEs that widens with scale, and small noisy activations are clipped to zero.

blocks.title: TopK on the pentagon SAE: choosing k

scenes.caption: Same input as lesson 2, x = (0.8, 0), same tied pentagon SAE but no bias. Pre-activations: 0.8 on latent 0, 0.247 leaks on latents 1 and 4.
k = 1 keeps 0.8 untouched. x-hat = (0.8, 0) exactly: squared error 0. No shrinkage, because nothing taxes the magnitude.
k = 2 also keeps a leak (0.247, tie broken toward latent 1). x-hat = (0.876, 0.235), error 0.061. Too large a k admits interference.
New input with two true features: x = 0.8 d0 + 0.6 d1 = (0.985, 0.571). Pre-activations 0.985, 0.847, -0.462, -1.133, -0.238.
k = 1 keeps only latent 0: x-hat = (0.985, 0), error 0.326. A fixed k cannot adapt when a token genuinely has more features.

blocks.prompt: In the last scene, k = 2 would keep both correct latents, at 0.985 and 0.847. The true strengths are 0.8 and 0.6. Will reconstruction be perfect?
blocks.reveal: No. x-hat = (1.247, 0.806), squared error 0.124. The tied encoder reads each latent with a plain dot product, so the +0.309 overlap between neighbours inflates both readings. Re-fitting the two magnitudes by least squares on the chosen support gives exactly 0.8 and 0.6. Trained encoders learn rows that partly cancel such interference, and Gao et al. use this kind of refinement to measure leftover bias. Simplified: a real SAE's encoder is learned, not tied to the decoder.

blocks.md:
**Gated SAEs** (Rajamanoharan et al., DeepMind 2024) split the encoder into a gate path that decides which latents are on and a magnitude path that sets their size, sharing weights between the two. The L1 penalty is applied only to the gate, so magnitudes are not shrunk. They report needing about half as many firing latents for the same reconstruction fidelity.

**JumpReLU SAEs** (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024) keep a normal elementwise encoder but give every latent $i$ its own learned threshold $\theta_i$. Below the threshold the latent is 0; above it, the value passes through unchanged. Unlike TopK, the number of active latents can vary from token to token.

blocks.caption: H is the Heaviside step. The penalty is a true L0 count, trained using straight-through estimators: pseudo-derivatives for theta built from a narrow kernel of bandwidth epsilon around the threshold.

scenes.caption: Plain ReLU passes the 0.247 interference leak through: too many latents fire.
A negative bias is ReLU(z - theta): leaks below theta are removed, but every surviving value is shifted down by theta. That is the shrinkage from lesson 2.
JumpReLU with theta = 0.4 zeroes the 0.247 leak yet passes 0.8 through unchanged, so the pentagon example reconstructs exactly with L0 = 1.
Each latent learns its own theta. A higher threshold means fewer firings; lambda on the L0 term controls how hard training pushes thresholds up.

blocks.md: DeepMind reports that at a fixed L0 on Gemma 2 9B, JumpReLU SAEs reconstruct at least as well as TopK and better than Gated SAEs, while being cheaper to train than either: one forward and backward pass with an elementwise activation, no partial sort. JumpReLU is the architecture behind Gemma Scope. In the JumpReLU paper the bandwidth $\varepsilon = 0.001$ worked well across layers and sites, assuming activations normalised to unit mean squared norm.

L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.
TopK fixes L0 = k on every token, even when a token needs more or fewer features. JumpReLU and L1 SAEs let L0 vary, so their reported L0 is an average over tokens.

blocks.question: You switch an SAE from L1 to TopK and keep everything else the same. Which hyperparameter replaces lambda as the main sparsity knob?
options: The learning rate
The number of latents M
k, the number of latents kept per token
The kernel bandwidth epsilon
blocks.explain: TopK sets sparsity directly: L0 equals k. There is no sparsity term in the loss, so there is no lambda to tune. Epsilon belongs to JumpReLU training.

blocks.question: An L1 SAE's latents look right on inspection, but its reconstructions are consistently a bit too short (smaller norm than x). What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Dead latents; resample them
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; use TopK, JumpReLU or a Gated SAE, or re-fit magnitudes on the chosen latents
The learning rate is too high; lower it
The dictionary is too large; reduce M
blocks.explain: L1 pulls every active magnitude down by about lambda/2 (in the one-latent case), so x-hat is systematically small. Architectures that decouple selection from magnitude remove this bias.

lessons.title: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting

blocks.md:
A **dead latent** never activates. It wastes a column of the dictionary and its compute. Anthropic and OpenAI both call a latent dead if it has not fired over 10 million tokens.

Death happens because a latent whose pre-activation is negative on every input gets no gradient through the ReLU (or never makes the top k), so nothing pulls it back. It gets worse with width: more latents compete to explain the same data.

scenes.caption: Towards Monosemanticity, run A/1: 168 of 4,096 latents dead (4.1%), with dead-latent resampling already on. Another 292 (7.1%) fired on under 1 in a million examples.
Scaling Monosemanticity on Claude 3 Sonnet: roughly 2%, 35% and 65% dead as the dictionary grows from 1M to 4M to 34M. The 34M SAE had about 12M live latents.

OpenAI saw up to 90% dead latents in ablations without mitigations, but with their two fixes only 7% of the 16M-latent GPT-4 SAE was dead. Different models and recipes, so compare trends, not exact values.

blocks.md:
Three fixes appear in the papers:

1. **Resampling** (Towards Monosemanticity): periodically find latents that have not fired for many steps and reset their encoder weights toward inputs the SAE currently reconstructs badly.
2. **Encoder initialised to the decoder's transpose** (Gao et al.): each latent starts out detecting the same direction it writes, so it begins life near data it can explain.
3. **AuxK auxiliary loss** (Gao et al., similar to Anthropic's 'ghost grads'): make the dead latents try to explain what the live ones missed.

blocks.caption: z_dead keeps the top k_aux pre-activations among latents flagged dead (typically k_aux = 512, alpha = 1/32). Dead latents now receive gradient from the residual error.

blocks.title: One TopK training step with AuxK
blocks.code:
z_pre = W_enc @ (x - b_pre)            # [M]
z = topk(z_pre, k)                      # main latents
x_hat = W_dec @ z + b_pre
loss = sum((x - x_hat) ** 2)

steps_since_fired[z > 0] = 0
steps_since_fired[z == 0] += tokens_per_step
dead = steps_since_fired > 10_000_000

if dead.any():
    e = x - x_hat                       # what the live latents missed
    z_dead = topk(where(dead, z_pre, -inf), k_aux)
    e_hat = W_dec @ z_dead
    loss += alpha * sum((e - e_hat) ** 2)

loss.backward(); adam.step()
normalize_columns(W_dec)               # unit-norm decoder

scenes.caption: Normal TopK forward pass: encode, keep k, decode, squared error. Only the k chosen latents receive gradient.
Track how long each latent has been silent. Latents silent for 10 million tokens are flagged dead.
AuxK: take the residual error and reconstruct it using only the top k_aux dead latents. Their best guesses now get gradient.
Update, then keep decoder columns unit norm (one of several conventions). Gao et al. report AuxK adds only about 10% compute because the encoder pass is shared.

blocks.md:
**Feature splitting** is the second scale effect. Train SAEs of different widths on the same activations and compare. Towards Monosemanticity found that features come in families: going from 512 latents (A/0) to 4,096 (A/1) to 16,384 (A/2), the number of latents specific to base64 text went from 1 to 3 to many more.

A coarse latent that fires on 'the' in mathematical prose (A/0/341) predicts generic maths tokens such as 'the theorem'. Wider runs contain more specific relatives: a machine-learning version (A/2/15021) predicting 'the dataset', an abstract algebra and topology version (A/2/4878) predicting 'the quotient', and a gravitation and field theory version (A/2/2609) predicting 'the Lagrangian'.

blocks.title: Feature splitting as the dictionary grows

scenes.caption: A 512-latent dictionary has one broad latent for 'the' in technical maths writing. Its top predicted next tokens are generic: the denominator, the remainder, the theorem.
The 16,384-latent run has specific relatives with specific predictions (the classifier; the subgroup; the spacetime). Simplified: the paper finds splits and merges, not a clean tree.
Counts for base64 contexts across widths: 1, then 3, then many. More capacity buys finer distinctions of the same territory.

blocks.prompt: If wider SAEs keep splitting features into finer ones, what is the 'correct' number of latents for an SAE on a given layer?
blocks.reveal: There probably is not one. Towards Monosemanticity conjectures an idealised set of very many fine features, of which any finite dictionary returns a coarser covering. Width is then a resolution knob: small SAEs give a summary, large ones give detail. Gemma Scope releases a ladder of widths on the same site (2^14 to 2^19 latents on some layers) precisely so researchers can study this.

blocks.md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.
A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

blocks.question: Your 4M-latent SAE has 40% dead latents. Which change directly gives those latents a training signal?
options: Increase lambda so the remaining latents are sparser
Add an auxiliary loss that reconstructs the main SAE's residual error using only the dead latents' top activations
Decrease the batch size
Remove the decoder bias
blocks.explain: A dead latent gets no gradient from the main loss because it never fires. AuxK forces the top k_aux dead latents to predict the residual error, giving them gradient toward directions the live latents miss. Increasing lambda would push even more latents off.

blocks.question: You compare a 4,096-latent and a 65,536-latent SAE on the same layer. The smaller one has a 'Python code' latent; the larger has several latents for different Python contexts and none that matches it exactly. What does this indicate?
options: The larger SAE is broken
Feature splitting: the wider dictionary covers the same concept at finer resolution
The smaller SAE has dead latents
Python is not represented in the model
blocks.explain: This is the expected pattern from Towards Monosemanticity: wider dictionaries refine broad latents into families of more specific ones.

lessons.title: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features

blocks.md:
Three numbers summarise an SAE (definitions as in Gemma Scope and Gao et al.):

- **L0**: the average number of active latents per token, $\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\|_0$. Lower is sparser and usually easier to interpret.
- **Fraction of variance unexplained (FVU)**, which OpenAI calls normalised MSE: reconstruction MSE divided by the MSE of always predicting the mean activation. **Fraction of variance explained** is $1 - \text{FVU}$.
- **Downstream loss**: splice $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ into the model in place of $\mathbf{x}$, keep running the forward pass, and measure next-token cross-entropy. **Delta LM loss** is the increase over the clean model.

blocks.caption: Loss recovered compares the SAE to zero-ablating the activation: 100% means the SAE is as good as the real activation.

blocks.title: Computing L0 and FVU on a 4-token batch (pentagon TopK SAE)

scenes.caption: Four activations: t0 = 0.8 d0, t1 = 0.8 d0 + 0.6 d1, t2 = 0.5 d3, t3 = 0. Their mean is (0.345, 0.069); the baseline MSE of predicting it is 0.423.
TopK with k = 1. L0 per token 1, 1, 1, 0 (the zero token activates nothing), mean L0 = 0.75. Only t1 has error (0.326): it has two features. MSE 0.081, FVU 0.193, so 80.7% of variance explained.
k = 2. Mean L0 = 1.5. t1 improves to 0.124 but t0 and t2 now admit interference latents. MSE 0.052, FVU 0.123 (87.7% explained). Doubling L0 bought 7 points of variance.

blocks.md:
Published numbers for scale: Scaling Monosemanticity's three Sonnet SAEs had fewer than 300 active latents per token on average and explained at least 65% of the variance. Towards Monosemanticity's A/1 recovered 79% of the loss reduction the MLP layer provides; its 131,072-latent run A/5 recovered 94.5%.

Gao et al. warn that loss recovered flatters SAEs on the residual stream: zero-ablating the whole residual stream is catastrophic, so even poor SAEs score high. Their 16M GPT-4 SAE scored 98.2% on that metric, yet substituting it into GPT-4 gave a loss matching a model trained with about 10% of GPT-4's pretraining compute.

blocks.prompt: Illustrative numbers: the clean model's loss is 3.00 nats, with your SAE spliced in it is 3.20, and with the residual stream zeroed it is 10.0. What is the loss recovered, and is this SAE good?
blocks.reveal: $(10.0 - 3.20)/(10.0 - 3.00) = 97.1\%$, which sounds excellent. But delta LM loss is 0.20 nats, a large degradation for a language model. Gemma Scope uses delta LM loss as its primary fidelity metric, and notes residual-stream SAEs show higher delta loss than MLP or attention SAEs even at similar FVU, since small residual errors propagate through every later layer.

blocks.md:
These metrics trade off: lower L0 or fewer latents means higher error. Gao et al. fit a **scaling law** for TopK SAEs on GPT-4 at convergence, in the number of latents $n$ and sparsity $k$ (natural logs; it holds only for small $k$):

$L(n,k) = e^{\alpha + \beta_k \ln k + \beta_n \ln n + \gamma \ln k \ln n} + e^{\zeta + \eta \ln k}$

with $\alpha = -0.50$, $\beta_k = 0.26$, $\beta_n = -0.017$, $\gamma = -0.042$, $\zeta = -1.32$, $\eta = -0.085$. The second term is an irreducible floor that falls only as $k$ grows.

blocks.title: Normalised MSE vs number of latents (Gao et al. GPT-4 fit)

scenes.caption: k = 32: FVU falls from 0.533 at 10K latents to 0.299 at 16M (about 2^24). Each 10x more latents helps less.
k = 512: 0.392 at 10K and 0.187 at 16M. More active latents lowers both the curve and the floor, at the cost of a denser, harder-to-read code.
k = 16: 0.576 at 10K, 0.347 at 16M. The negative gamma makes the curve flatter for small k: very sparse codes gain less from extra width.

blocks.md:
**Steering** tests whether a latent is causal, not just correlated. Scaling Monosemanticity's recipe: split the residual activation into the SAE reconstruction and the error, $\mathbf{x} = \text{SAE}(\mathbf{x}) + \text{error}(\mathbf{x})$. Replace SAE(x) with a version in which latent $i$ is clamped to a chosen value $c$, keep the error term unchanged, and run the downstream layers on the result, at every token position.

Because the decoder is linear, clamping is the same as adding a scaled copy of the latent's direction:

blocks.caption: Keeping the error term means everything the SAE fails to explain is left untouched; only the chosen feature changes.

blocks.title: Clamping latent 3 to 2.0 in the pentagon SAE

scenes.caption: Token t1 from before with k = 2: latents 0 and 1 active, reconstruction (1.247, 0.806), error (-0.262, -0.235).
Clamp latent 3 from 0 to 2.0. The new reconstruction is (-0.371, -0.370).
Add back the unchanged error: x' = (-0.633, -0.605), exactly x + 2.0 d3. This vector replaces x in all later layers.

blocks.md:
In Claude 3 Sonnet, clamping a Golden Gate Bridge latent to 10 times its maximum observed activation made the model describe itself as the bridge; clamping a transit-infrastructure latent to 5 times its maximum made it mention a bridge where it otherwise would not. Clamping a code-error latent produced hallucinated error messages on bug-free code. The authors also built few-shot steering vectors from mean activation differences and found them generally less interpretable and less effective than feature steering in their case studies.

Other uses: Cunningham et al. patched SAE features to localise model behaviour on the indirect object identification task more precisely than with PCA directions, and Gemma Scope releases SAEs on every layer for circuit-style analysis.

Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

blocks.question: Two SAEs on the same residual-stream layer: A has L0 = 40 and FVU = 0.30; B has L0 = 400 and FVU = 0.10. Which conclusion is justified from these numbers alone?
options: B is strictly better because its FVU is lower
A is strictly better because it is sparser
Neither dominates; compare them on the same L0 or the same FVU, and check delta LM loss
They must have the same downstream loss because they share a layer
blocks.explain: SAEs live on a sparsity versus fidelity frontier. B buys lower error with ten times more active latents. Fair comparisons hold one axis fixed, and downstream loss can rank SAEs differently from MSE.

blocks.question: Why does the Scaling Monosemanticity steering recipe keep the SAE error term instead of feeding the edited reconstruction alone into later layers?
options: To make the latent's activation non-negative
So the only change to the activation is the chosen feature; dropping the error would also remove everything the SAE fails to reconstruct
Because the error term is always zero for TopK SAEs
To reduce memory use
blocks.explain: Replacing x with the reconstruction alone would apply two edits at once: the feature clamp and the loss of all unexplained structure. Keeping the error makes x' = x + (c - f_i) d_i.

blocks.question: You clamp a latent to a large negative value although the encoder never outputs negatives. What happens to the activation?
options: Nothing; negative clamps are clipped to zero
A negative multiple of the latent's decoder direction is added to x
The latent's decoder direction is deleted
All other latents are set to zero
blocks.explain: Scaling Monosemanticity notes that clamping to a negative value simply gives a negative multiple of the feature vector. In their code-error example, negative clamping made the model predict the output the code would have produced without the bug.
